title: Bronchiolitis (India, IAP)
subject: paediatrics
setting: Primary care, emergency department, paediatric ward, PICU
summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 2 years with coryza followed by cough, fast breathing, recession and wheeze or crackles. Care is supportive: nasal saline and suction, feeding support, oxygen below SpO2 90% (92% under 6 weeks or with comorbidity), and CPAP or high-flow for impending failure; antibiotics, steroids and routine bronchodilators have no role.

sections.title: Diagnose clinically
items: Coryza for 1 to 3 days, then persistent cough, tachypnoea with or without chest recession, and wheeze and/or crackles in a child under 2 years (usually under 1 year, peak 3 to 6 months).
Fever (usually below 39°C) in about 30%; poor feeding and vomiting typically after 3 to 5 days. Apnoea may be the only sign under 6 weeks.
RSV causes most cases (30 to 70% in Indian studies); rhinovirus, parainfluenza, adenovirus, metapneumovirus and bocavirus also cause it.
Think of pneumonia if fever is above 39°C with persistent focal crackles, and episodic viral wheeze if there is wheeze without crackles or recurrent episodes.

Severe disease: observed apnoea, marked distress (grunting, severe indrawing, respiratory rate above 70/min), central cyanosis, or SpO2 below 90% (over 6 weeks) or below 92% (under 6 weeks or with underlying conditions).

Higher risk: prematurity (especially below 32 weeks), low birth weight, age under 6 to 12 weeks, chronic lung disease, haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease; also passive smoke, crowding and day care.

sections.title: Investigations
items: No routine blood tests or chest X-ray. Use pulse oximetry to detect hypoxia and guide admission.
In admitted, more severe infants consider blood gas, CBC, CRP, electrolytes and chest X-ray, mainly to exclude bacterial pneumonia, heart failure or sepsis.
Viral testing rarely changes management; in hospital it may help avoid antibiotics and prevent cross-infection.

sections.title: Admit if
items: Persistent respiratory rate above 60/min, grunting or recession.
Oral intake 50 to 75% of usual or less, inability to feed, or dehydration.
SpO2 below 92% in room air, apnoea, or the child looks seriously unwell.
Carer unable to cope at home or living far from hospital.

sections.title: Supportive treatment
items: Clear the nose with saline drops and gentle suction (suction the upper airway for apnoea, secretions or feeding difficulty); nurse propped up with the head end elevated; paracetamol for fever.
Feeding: orogastric or nasogastric feeds if intake is poor; IV fluids only with impending respiratory failure or intolerance of tube feeds.
Oxygen if SpO2 is below 90% (over 6 weeks) or below 92% (under 6 weeks or with underlying conditions).
CPAP for impending respiratory failure; high-flow nasal cannula oxygen as rescue therapy may reduce the need for intensive care.

Optional, low value: nebulised hypertonic saline for infants in hospital longer than 3 days; nebulised adrenaline 0.1 to 0.3 mL/kg per dose of 1:1000 as rescue (short-lived benefit); a single trial of a beta-agonist, continued only if there is objective improvement.
No role for antibiotics, antivirals, systemic or inhaled steroids, montelukast, ipratropium, chest physiotherapy, steam inhalation, or palivizumab in the acute illness.

sections.title: Discharge and home advice
items: Discharge when clinically stable, feeding at least 75% of usual, and SpO2 in room air above 90% (over 6 weeks) or 92% (under 6 weeks or with comorbidity), with a carer able to cope who understands red flags.
Return at once for increased work of breathing (grunting, nasal flaring, recession), intake below 50 to 75% of normal or no urine for 12 hours, apnoea or cyanosis, or exhaustion.
Complications to watch for: secondary bacterial infection, myocarditis, heart failure, arrhythmia, ARDS and later bronchiolitis obliterans or recurrent wheeze.

sections.title: Prevention
items: Breastfeeding (non-breastfed infants have about 3 times the risk), hand hygiene, and avoiding passive smoke.

Palivizumab 15 mg/kg IM every 30 days through the RSV season (usually up to 5 doses) for infants under 12 months born before 29 weeks, with chronic lung disease of prematurity, or haemodynamically significant heart disease.
Nirsevimab, a single-dose antibody covering about 5 months, was under evaluation when the IAP STG was written.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Prescribing antibiotics, steroids or repeated salbutamol nebulisation without response.
Sending home a young infant whose feeding is below half of normal.
Missing apnoea as the presenting sign in infants under 6 weeks.
Over-reliance on SpO2 while ignoring work of breathing and fatigue.

drugs.name: Oxygen
drugs.dose: To keep SpO2 at or above 90% (over 6 weeks) or 92% (under 6 weeks or comorbidity)
drugs.notes: CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula for impending respiratory failure.

drugs.name: Palivizumab (prophylaxis)
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg IM every 30 days during the RSV season, up to 5 doses
drugs.notes: High-risk infants under 12 months; no role in acute illness.
